::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Is there a difference between theorem proof and theorem demonstration?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2057072/is-there-a-difference-between-theorem-proof-and-theorem-demonstration), asked by [yoyo_fun](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/325100/yoyo-fun) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-12-13; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> When referring to proving that a theorem is true, I have seen both words used interchangeably. Do they mean the same thing ?
:::

In English, *proof* and *demonstration* have different connotations, as Théophile points out.  A demonstration might be an application or “illustration” of a method.  I believe most native English speakers would use *proof*.

But in some other languages, the word cognate to *demonstration* is what is used for proof.  The letters QED, commonly appearing after a proof, are initials for the Latin phrase *quod erat demonstrandum*.  In French, they say *ce qu'il fallait démontrer*.  But in German, the word for “to prove” is *beweisen* rather than *demonstrieren* (and *prüfen* is to test!)
